lawyer:
Amir Hossain with Zakir Hussain Majumder, Advocates --- For the Appellants.
Abul Baset Majumder with SM Abul Hossain, Advocates --- For the Respondent.
parties:
Executive Engineer Sales and Distribution and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Purba Espat Limited ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 4-11-1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Comilla in Title Suit No. 62 of 1997. The learned Subordinate Judge by the said order directed the appellants to restore electricity connection of the plaintiff within 7 (seven) days from the date of the order. 

 2. The short fact leading to this appeal is that the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 62 of 1997 before the aforesaid court praying a declaration that the preparation and sending of bill in respect of power consumption by the plaintiff on the basis of a meter reading installed outside the premises is illegal, void without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff. The further case of the plaintiff is that they took electricity power connection in the plaintiff''s industry in 1994 and a meter was installed in the industry and the plaintiff was receiving regular bills for the consumption and making payments. Subsequently all on a sudden the plaintiff received three inflated bills the months of June, July and August 1997 for which he raised objection. It is the case of the plaintiff that these bills were sent on the basis of the alleged reading of a meter installed in the sub-station of the present appellant and after addition and subtraction of the power consumption by other consumers the balance was shifted upon the plaintiff which is illegal beyond jurisdiction and not covered by the contract. After the filing of the suit the plaintiff filed an application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and prayed for injunction restraining the defendants from disconnecting power consumption line of the plaintiff on the ground of non-payment of the disputed three bills and the trial Court by order dated 21-9-97 directed the defendants-appellants to show cause within three days from the date of receipt of the notice why they shall not be restrained by a temporary injunction in disconnecting the plaintiff''s power line pending disposal of the suit. It is also the case of the plaintiff that when the defendants came to know of this order to show cause they were taking preparation for disconnecting the power line and on receipt of the notice from the court and disregarding the protest made by the officers of the plaintiff and the information given to the defendants including the Magistrate the power consumption line of the plaintiff was disconnected on 22-9-97 at about 1-30 PM which compelled the plaintiff to file an application with a prayer for mandatory injunction. The trial Court it appears examined several witnesses from both the sides and by the impugned judgment and order directed the present appellants to restore the connection of the plaintiff within 7(seven) days from the date of the order. The contesting defendants on being aggrieved by this order dated 4-11-97 preferred this appeal. 

 3. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the suit was filed on 21-9-97 on which date the court directed the defendants-appellants to show cause why they shall not be restrained by an order of injunction from disconnecting the plaintiff''s power line within three days from the date of receipt of the notice. But as the plaintiff failed to pay the bills  for three months the power line was disconnected on 21-9-97 before the receipt of the notice from the court. He submits that notice was served upon the defendants 11-00 AM on 22-9-97. The learned Advocate the appellants contends that in such a suit where the consumer is bound to pay the bill a mandatory injunction cannot be granted where there is non-payment of such bills. If any party is aggrieved by any such bill he may approach the appropriate authority of the Power Development Board and may refer the matter to the Inspector of the electricity whose decision will be final. The learned Advocate contends that by avoiding the procedure the plaintiff filed the present suit and prayed for an injunction. 

 4. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff respondent on the other hand submits that whether the suit itself is maintainable or not will be decided at the time of trial and this will require examination of witnesses. He submits that when the trial Court has issued a notice and when the civil Court is seizing of the matter and when the defendants were fully aware of the pendency of the suit before the learned Subordinate Judge those appellants committed illegality in snapping the connection of the plaintiff. They ought to have waited for the decision of the trial Court in the matter. The learned Advocate the plaintiff contends that before the trial Court both the parties adduced oral evidence and it appears from the consideration of the evidence on record that the appellants were fully aware of the pendency of the suit on 21-9-97 but disregarding the pendency of the suit the power line was disconnected. The learned Advocate submits that a contingent of police force along with a Magistrate and PDB officials went to disconnect the power line and they were informed of the pendency of the suit. But inspite of this and inspite of the fact of receipt of the notice the power line was disconnected on 22-9-97. It is contended that the trial Court rightly passed the order of mandatory injunction. 

 5. Admittedly, the plaintiff has industry where in on a contract the defendant-appellants started supplying power from 1994 and a meter was installed in the premises of the industry and on the basis of meter reading the bills were being sent to the plaintiff which they paid accordingly. The dispute started when according to the plaintiff the defendants sent inflated bills for the months of June, July and August 1997. It is the case of the plaintiff that the maximum bill that was received by the plaintiff before June 1997 was of Taka 1,80,000.00 and odd, but suddenly it rose to Taka 7,00,000.00 from June 1997. The matter was brought to the notice of the present appellants for redress but without success which compelled the plaintiff to institute the present suit. It is the case of the plaintiff that instead of sending the bill on the basis of the meter reading installed in the industry the defendants installed a meter in their sub-station and by deducting the power consumed by other consumers the remaining amount was charged in the bill sent to the plaintiff which is illegal and against natural justice. 

 6. Admittedly the defendants are responsible for supplying power to the plaintiff on a contract and for calculation of the consumption a meter was installed in the premises of the plaintiff. From the sub-station to the meter the line is being maintained by the defendants. It is their property. That cannot be interfered with by any 3rd party nor even by the consumers. The responsibility of the defendant is to supply power and to maintain the line from the main line up to the meter and beyond the meter it is the responsibility of the consumer. If there is any defect in the consumer''s section and for that if the consumption is shown higher then the consumer is to pay for it. The supplier will not be responsible for that. But if there is any defect in the line from the main line to the meter then it is the responsibility of the supplier. It appears from the perusal of the record that the contesting defendants 1, 2, 5 and 6 have already submitted written statement and their case is found in paragraph No.10 of the same. From this paragraph No.10 it appears that due to certain defects and suspecting that the consumption of power by the plaintiff would be more the defendant installed another meter in the Courtbari sub-station and they have also installed another meter at Choto Alampur and by deducting the power consumed as shown in the meter installed at Choto Alampur they have charged the plaintiff. It appears from the written statement that there are certain defects in the power consumption line of the defendants portion for which there was less showing in the installed meter at the plaintiff''s premises. That there was any defect in the plaintiff''s installation there is no allegation or that there was certain pilferage of power by the plaintiff. There is also no allegation in the written statement. It has also been stated in the written statement that the Inspector of Electricity examined the mater installed in the plaintiff''s industry as well as the two other meters and all these meters were found to be in order. Prima facie when there is any defect in the power line from the sub-satiation to the meter installed in the premises of the consumer and for that matter if there is less reading in the meter for that the consumer cannot be prima facie made liable. Furthermore in the Electricity Act or the Rules made thereunder there is nothing to show that such meters may be installed at different places and by addition sub-station bills may be sent to the consumers. If there is any defect in the power line that should be checked and corrected by the supplier and if required cost of such repairing in appropriate cases may be realised form the consumer. But for that matter separate meter cannot be installed. It has not been stated in the written statement that from the sub-station to the plaintiff''s installation there is no other connection. The defendants are resident on this point. It is not the case in the written statement that no other consumer has been connected from that line. In such a situation prima facie it appears that the plaintiff is to be charged from the reading of the meter installed in his installation. If any deviation is to be made from the normal procedure it must be with the prior knowledge and consent of the consumer. The meter is installed in a premises for finding out the quantum of power consumed and the Rules provided  that it must be sealed by the Power Development Board. But if at the instance of the consumers the seal is broken the consumer is to be penalized. But such a meter cannot be installed at a place out side the installation where there may be scope for giving connections to other consumers much to the prejudice of the consumer where the meter has been installed. So prima facie it appears that the steps taken by the defendants is not in accordance with law. From the written statement and from the submission made by the learned Advocate for the appellants it appears that the system was device for detecting pilferage by the consumer. But prima facie it indicates that there is scope for pilferage from the other end and for that matter before finalization of the dispute as regards this inflated bills the consumption line of the plaintiff ought not to have been disconnected. 

 7. Section 26 of the Electricity Act provides that in the absence of an agreement to the contrary the amount of energy supplied to a consumer or the electrical quantity contained in the supply shall be ascertained by means of a correct meter and the licensee shall, if required by the consumer, cause the consumer to be supplied with such a meter. Here in the present case the consumer was supplied the meter and it is presumed that it is a correct meter. Subsection (2) of this section further provides that where the consumer so enters into an agreement for the hire of a meter the licensee shall keep the meter correct and in default of his doing so the consumer shall for so long as the default continues ceases to be liable to pay for the hire of the meter. Admittedly, the present meter has been installed by the defendants and law provides that they are to supply a correct meter and from the written statement it appears that the meter installed in the premises is a correct one and from sub-section (1) it appears that for the consumption the meter installed in the plaintiff''s installation should be the right meter from which it can be found how much power has been consumed by plaintiff-consumer. Sub-section (4) of this section further provides that the licensee or any person duly authorized by the licensee shall at any reasonable time and informing the consumer of his intention have access to and be at liberty to inspect and test and for that purpose if he thinks fit, Jake off and remove any meter referred to in sub-section (1) and, except where the meter is so hired as-aforesaid all reasonable expenses of and incidental to, such inspecting testing, taking off and removing shall if the meter is found to be otherwise than correct he recovered from the consumer and where any difference or dispute arises as to amount of such reasonable expenses the matter shall be referred to an Electric Inspector and the decision of such Inspector shall be final. The earlier portion of sub-section (4) gave the appellants all the power to inspect the meter installed at the premises of the consumer at any reasonable time on informing the consumer. The second part is in respect of the meter which is owned by the consumer. Here in the present case the meter installed in the plaintiff''s industry is owned by the appellants and they have all the access to it and if they find that there is no correct reading they may correct it. But here in the present case the meter that was installed was found to be correct. It is the definite case of the appellants that as the meter was not giving correct reading and as they suspected that the consumption ought to have been much higher they installed two separate meters, one in the Court Bari sub-station and another at Choto Alampur. But sub-section (7) of section 26 of the aforesaid Act provides that in addition to any meter which may be placed upon the premises of a consumer in pursuance of the provisions of subsection (1), the licensee may place upon such premises such meter maximum demand indicator or other apparatus as he may think fit for the purpose of ascertaining or regulating either the amount of energy supplied to the consumer or the number of hours during which the supply is given or the rate per unit of time at which energy is supplied to the consumer, or any other quantity or time connected with the supply. It has been provided that the meter, indicator or apparatus shall not in the absence of an agreement to the contrary be placed otherwise then between the distributing mains of the licensee''s and any meter referred to in .sub-section (1). This clearly indicates that the meter must be installed in the premises and for checking or rechecking other apparatus may be installed in the premises in addition to the meter already installed under sub-section (1). So prima facie it indicates that no such meter may be installed in the sub-station. From a consideration of the provisions of section 26 of the said Act particularly sub-sections (1),(2), (4) and (7) it appears that the stand taken by the appellants is not supported by the law. So prima facie it appears that on the basis of the meter installed at Choto Alampur and in the sub-station the plaintiff cannot be charged. It is not the case of the appellants that the meter installed at the premises was tampered with by the consumer. Thus far is the legal position. 

 8. Now as regards the disconnection it is the definite case of the appellants that the suit was filed on 21-9-97 and then before the receipt of the notice they disconnected the power line on that date at about 1-30 PM. The plaintiff''s definite case is that the power line was snapped on 22-9-97 after the receipt of the notice and also when they were informed verbally when the officials of the defendants, the Magistrate and the police went to disconnect the power line. Before the trial Court it appears 6 witnesses from the side of the plaintiff have been examined and all of them deposed that the line was snapped on 22-9-97 and not on 21-9-97 as in the case of the appellants. Out of the 6 (six) witnesses the plaintiff examined PW 2-4 as local witnesses and they consistently and uniformly deposed that the line was disconnected on 22-9-97 at 12-00/12-30 mid day. Of them PW 4 is member of the Union Parishad who supported the plaintiff''s case. The plaintiff also examined the Magistrate who accompanied the appellant''s officials to disconnect the power line as PW 6. He also in his examination-in-chief deposed that he worked with the PDB which went to disconnect power line on 22-9-91. This witness it appears tried to suppress some facts which are definitely in the official record which he failed to produce before the trial Court in support of the defence contention that power line was snapped on 21-9-97. From the side of the defence only one witness was examined who is defendant No.5. He of course deposed that the line was disconnected on 21-9-97. Though the trial Court while passing the impugned order has not discussed the oral evidence between consideration of the evidence on record hold that the plaintiff succeeded pima facie to prove that the power line was disconnected on 22-9-97 and not on 21-9-97 as alleged by the appellants. That the appellants were aware of the pendency of the injunction matter and the show cause will also be evident from the return of the process server who stated that on 21-9-97 he went to the office of the defendant for serving the notice of the injunction but was asked to go there on the following day. The non-acceptance of the notice on 21-9-97 goes a long way to show the attitude of the defendants in the matter. 

 9. Admittedly, the plaintiff consumed the power in the months of June, July and August 1997. There is no doubt about it. Now the question is how much amount is to be paid by them will be decided at the time of trial. Admittedly the highest amount of the bill was in the month of April which was not Taka 1,08,549.20 and when the plaintiff has consumed the power for June, July and August 1997 they should pay the highest amount of each three months from before disconnection. The fate of the bills sent by the defendants appellants for the month of June, July and August will be decided at the time of trial. But for the time being the plaintiff must pay at the highest rate of consumption for the month of April for these three months and we are inclined to direct the plaintiff to deposit Taka 3,35,000.00 with the trial Court before restoration of the power line. 

 10. Mr Abdul Baset Majumder the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents submits that the plaintiff is an industry and due to the disconnection the industry is suffering and they are not in a position to pay salaries and other benefits to their employees and they are also losing their market and they have certain foreign experts and for the stoppage of industry due to non-supply of power the industry is suffering and as such the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of the plaintiff. If the plaintiff gets relief in the suit they may realize their dues from the plaintiff and the law has provided that such dues may be realised under certificate proceeding. 

 11. Having given our anxious consideration to the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides we hold that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of the plaintiff and we also hold that the trial Court has not committed any illegality or wrong in passing the impugned order. There is therefore, no merit in this appeal. 

 13. The appeal is accordingly dismissed with the cost. The judgment and order passed by the trial Court on 4-11-1997 is hereby affirmed. The plaintiff-respondent is hereby directed to deposit a sum of Taka 3,25,000.00 with the trial Court within 2(two) weeks from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment from this court and the appellants will be at liberty to withdraw the amount from the court if they so desire. The appellants are hereby directed to restore the power supply to the plaintiff''s installation within 7 (seven) days from the date of deposit of the aforesaid amount by the plaintiff with the trial Court, in default the plaintiff will be at liberty to execute the order through court.
